newsitem.title: POLAND: PRESIDENT FIRES CONTROVERSIAL POLISH ARMY CHIEF.
newsitem.headline: PRESIDENT FIRES CONTROVERSIAL POLISH ARMY CHIEF.

text.p: Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski will sack the armed forces Chief of Staff General Tadeusz Wilecki, the presidential spokesman said on Monday.

"The president will dismiss General Wilecki... and appoint General Henryk Szumski in his place," spokesman Antoni Styrczula told Reuters, adding that further details would be given at a news conference.

Critics have long accused Wilecki of seeking to entrench the general staff's authority at the expense of the defence ministry and of harming Poland's bid to fully meet exacting standards for civilian control of the armed forces required by NATO from aspiring new members.
Poland expects, along with the Czechs and Hungarians, to be in the first wave of countries invited at NATO's July summit in Madrid to start talks on joining the pact.

Wilecki's differences with the dominant party in the ruling coalition, Kwasniewski's ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), exploded into an open row last week, when the head of the SLD's parliament caucus said it was time for him to go.

Wilecki denies he has undermined civilian control of the military while arguing that he has provided vital stability of leadership and battled for adequate funds as the army prepared for NATO entry through years of changing governments and ministers.

"If anyone tries to change the leadership of the Polish army five minutes before the process of integration with NATO, I ask why?...I think one should not change the team at such a fraught moment," Wilecki told a public radio interviewer shortly before his dismissal was announced.
Wilecki's row with the dominant parliamentary party dates from late 1994 when general staff officers at a lunch in the Drawsko training ground reportedly voted to remove the then defence minister.

Lech Walesa, Polish president at the time, who was present and sympathetic to army staff views, sacked the minister -- arousing concerns in Poland and in NATO that parliamentary control of the military was not adequately established.
Last year, however, there was a major reform of Poland's command and control structures, entrenching the defence ministry's position.
Wilecki rejected arguments that he had undermined Poland's NATO case, saying that under his leadership the military had drawn very close to the armies of the Western pact.

"This is a very painful argument for us, because it is us who have brought Poland closer to NATO...therefore it is hard to accuse us of standing on the road to NATO entry," Wilecki told the radio interviewer.

Switching to the attack, he accused the SLD of reneging on promises made in February 1995 that it would bring spending on the military up to three percent of Gross Domestic Product and said it was still only at 2.3 percent -- preventing vital modernisation and condemning army families to hardship.
"I have to say, with sadness, that certain obligations made above all by the left have not been honoured," he said.
Wilecki has received support over the past week from parts of the right-leaning opposition and from the Polish Peasant party (PSL), the SLD's smaller partner in the ruling coalition.
